{"id": "20:125/q13", "question": "What aspects of Qur'anic coherence and expression does Suyuti study?", "turns_on": "These are complementary topics in Suyuti's program, not competing explanations of this verse.", "positions": [{"id": "20:125/q13/p1", "position": "He studies how verse endings suit their verses.", "reasons": "Suyuti names this as one dimension of coherence."}, {"id": "20:125/q13/p2", "position": "He studies how a surah's name relates to its contents.", "reasons": "Suyuti includes this among the topics of coherence."}, {"id": "20:125/q13/p3", "position": "He explains why one synonym is selected over another.", "reasons": "Suyuti presents this as a question of Qur'anic word choice."}, {"id": "20:125/q13/p4", "position": "He studies famous and anomalous readings and their meanings as part of inimitability.", "reasons": "Suyuti explicitly includes knowledge of readings in his method."}, {"id": "20:125/q13/p5", "position": "He studies differences among repeated passages, including addition, omission, reordering and substituted words.", "reasons": "Suyuti lists these forms of variation."}, {"id": "20:125/q13/p6", "position": "He wrote a concise work on coherence in surah order, selecting views he approved.", "reasons": "Suyuti says the work was largely his own thinking because few had studied this subject; he renamed it Tanāsuq al-Durar from Nata'ij al-Fikr because the later title better fitted its subject and added wordplay."}]}
{"id": "20:125/q14", "question": "Was surah order set by prophetic instruction or Companion judgment?", "turns_on": "The differing early codex orders and the report of Uthman's arrangement favor Companion judgment; the account of Gabriel assigning each surah and verse its place supports prophetic instruction. Both sides agree on verse order.", "positions": [{"id": "20:125/q14/p1", "position": "Surah order came through the Companions' independent judgment.", "reasons": "Suyuti reports this as one side of the dispute, held by Malik, Qadi Abu Bakr in one opinion and decisively by Ibn Faris. Early codices differed: Ali's followed revelation order; Ibn Masud began al-Baqara, al-Nisa, Al Imran; Ubayy's and other codices differed too. Ibn Ashta transmits that Uthman ordered the long surahs together."}, {"id": "20:125/q14/p2", "position": "Surah order was fixed by prophetic instruction.", "reasons": "Suyuti reports another group including Qadi Abu Bakr's other opinion. Ibn al-Anbari says Gabriel showed the Prophet each surah's and verse's place after the Qur'an descended first to the lowest heaven and then over twenty-odd years; changing the sequence corrupts its order. Both sides agree verse order was instructed."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q01", "question": "What does the first كَذَٰلِكَ point to, and how is it construed?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of dhālika, the supplied expression, and whether the first kāf is extra or retains its ordinary comparative force.", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q01/p1", "position": "It points to the addressee's blind resurrection or his former conduct, which explains the present treatment.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya relates it to the blindness just mentioned. Al-Zamakhshari, as reported by al-Samin and al-Alusi, supplies 'you acted thus' and parses the kāf as a direct object; al-Alusi says it points to resurrection blind. Al-Nasafi likewise supplies the person's action. Ibn ʿAshur says the fate fits his refusal to consider the signs; al-Tabatabaʾi makes the reply an answer to his question about blindness, with recompense in kind (42:40). Al-Biqaʿi includes this as one alternative."}, {"id": "20:126/q01/p2", "position": "It affirms that matters are just as the person now sees or says, before the reply explains why.", "reasons": "Al-Wahidi says God answers 'this is how things are, as you see.' Al-Baydawi says God treated him in just that way and then explains it. Al-Biqaʿi offers 'matters were as he said' as an alternative, on which the reply supplies the cause."}, {"id": "20:126/q01/p3", "position": "It describes the way God's clear signs came to the person.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari glosses it 'thus they came to you.' Abu al-Baqa, reported by al-Samin, allows an arrival like that. Al-Alusi treats the kāf as extra, comparing mithluka lā yabkhal, and takes dhālika to indicate their striking manner of arrival; he contrasts al-Zamakhshari's nonextra kāf. Al-Samin says such estimates make the kāf accusative as verbal noun or direct object."}, {"id": "20:126/q01/p4", "position": "An omitted noun makes it mean a gathering of this kind.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa, as reported by al-Samin, supplies an omitted noun for the manner of gathering; al-Samin allows an accusative kāf under these estimates."}, {"id": "20:126/q01/p5", "position": "It can indicate retribution matching the person's turning away or forgetting.", "reasons": "Abu al-Baqa, reported by al-Samin, includes this among possible estimates; al-Samin allows the accusative kāf as verbal noun or direct object."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q02", "question": "What are the ءَايَٰتُنَا that came to the person?", "turns_on": "Whether the signs are specified as Qur'anic revelation, proofs of divine attributes, or the messenger's whole presentation of guidance.", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q02/p1", "position": "They are God's revealed signs, especially the Qur'an and its clarifying proofs.", "reasons": "Muqatil identifies Qur'anic signs. Al-Tabari calls them proofs, evidences, and clarification in God's Book. Al-Bursevi includes revealed verses and says the signs were clear to everyone. Al-Zamakhshari, reported by al-Samin, calls them clear and illuminating; al-Nasafi, al-Kashshaf, and al-Alusi also stress their clarity."}, {"id": "20:126/q02/p2", "position": "They are proofs of God's oneness and power.", "reasons": "Al-Qurtubi specifies proofs of oneness and power; al-Bursevi includes proofs of divine power and signs of oneness among the clear signs."}, {"id": "20:126/q02/p3", "position": "They include the message and proofs brought by God's messengers, specifically Muhammad and the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Al-Tabrisi names Muhammad, the Qur'an, and the proofs. The Study Quran calls them proofs brought by God's messengers."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q03", "question": "What does فَنَسِيتَهَا mean here?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q03/p1", "position": "He deliberately neglected, rejected, or failed to act on the signs, treating them as though forgotten.", "reasons": "Muqatil, Yahya, al-Wahidi, and Ibn al-Jawzi stress abandoning belief; al-Tabari adds rejection and failure to act, while al-Suddi specifies abandoning the duty to act. Mujahid glosses it as leaving the signs behind. Al-Kashshaf, al-Nasafi, al-Baydawi, al-Qurtubi, and Abu Hayyan stress failure to reflect or consider, turning away, and blindness to clear signs. Ibn Kathir says they were conveyed but deliberately ignored. Al-Biqaʿi invokes veiled eyes (18:101); al-Alusi says the effect, forgetting, is named for its cause, turning away. Al-Tabrisi and Ibn ʿAtiyya distinguish culpable neglect from an involuntary mental lapse. Al-Islahi says ignored revelation leaves the eyes shut."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q04", "question": "What does the second كَذَٰلِكَ say about the person's treatment?", "turns_on": "Whether the second kāf expresses a matching comparison or causal 'because of'.", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q04/p1", "position": "His treatment corresponds to his conduct: as he neglected the signs, God leaves him to the fitting consequence.", "reasons": "Al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj, al-Thaʿlabi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan, Ibn Kathir, al-Biqaʿi, al-Bursevi, al-Islahi, and al-Tabatabaʾi express requital in kind. Al-Alusi says the second dhālika points to the neglect implied by nasiya and the kāf retains its ordinary comparative sense; Ibn Kathir compares 7:51 and explicitly calls it recompense matching the deed; al-Tabatabaʾi cites 42:40. Al-Tabari treats Qatada's withholding of good as close to the Fire gloss, since the Fire is the greatest evil."}, {"id": "20:126/q04/p2", "position": "The kāf can mean 'because of': he is left because he neglected the signs.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports this from some interpreters and compares a proposed understanding of 'remember Him as He guided you' in 2:198."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q05", "question": "What does تُنسَىٰ mean for the person on that Day?", "turns_on": "The notes variously specify the resulting Fire, blindness, loss of good, or loss of mercy; al-Tabari explicitly treats the good/evil and Fire accounts as close.", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q05/p1", "position": "He is abandoned in the Fire or enduring punishment, without release or relief.", "reasons": "Muqatil adds that he is never brought out and is no longer remembered by God. Yahya, Ikrimah, Mujahid, Abu Salih, al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj, al-Thaʿlabi, al-Wahidi, al-Baghawi, Ibn al-Jawzi, al-Qurtubi, al-Durr, and Abu Hayyan identify the Fire or punishment. Al-Tabrisi says the punishment does not end. Al-Tabari says this is the greatest evil and close to Qatada's formulation. Al-Islahi says the complaint cannot reverse the deserved fate."}, {"id": "20:126/q05/p2", "position": "He is left blind or without sight and guidance, along with punishment.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf, al-Baydawi, Abu Hayyan's report of al-Zamakhshari, al-Biqaʿi, al-Bursevi, al-Alusi, and al-Tabatabaʾi connect the abandonment to blindness. Al-Nasafi says God leaves him to his deeds and does not lift the veil from his eyes. Al-Bursevi says blindness, muteness, and deafness are eventually removed so he sees the terrors and his place in Hell (19:38); al-Alusi similarly links later sight of the Fire to 18:53 and calls it punishment upon punishment."}, {"id": "20:126/q05/p3", "position": "He is deprived of good while evil or punishment is not withheld from him.", "reasons": "Qatada says he is forgotten as to good, not evil; al-Baghawi phrases it as forgetting what is good but not

{"id": "20:126/q06", "question": "Why is the person raised blind in the surrounding dialogue?", "turns_on": "Whether blindness is a direct matching requital or the persistence and intensification of the soul's acquired spiritual state.", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q06/p1", "position": "Resurrection blindness recompenses his former refusal to see or heed God's guidance.", "reasons": "Al-Razi gives this as one explanation. Al-Kashshaf, Ibn ʿAtiyya, al-Biqaʿi, Ibn ʿAshur, al-Tabatabaʾi, Asad, and al-Islahi relate worldly disregard to the blindness and the reply. Ibn ʿAshur says the blindness marks God's anger and exclusion from mercy; al-Islahi says ignored revelation shut their eyes and made their complaint useless."}, {"id": "20:126/q06/p2", "position": "The soul remains ignorant and cut off from spiritual beings after leaving the body, and its spiritual pain intensifies.", "reasons": "Al-Razi offers this as an alternative: worldly rejection of evidence produced that state, which persists after death."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q07", "question": "How do worldly and resurrection blindness relate?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q07/p1", "position": "Worldly blindness to guidance is figurative or unrecognized; resurrection blindness is real and recognized when reality is unveiled.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur explicitly distinguishes figurative first blindness from real blindness at resurrection. Al-Islahi reconciles the passage with 50:22: people did not recognize their worldly blindness but do when reality is unveiled. Al-Qushayri cites a report that one meets God in the state in which one lived, so blindness of heart and ignorance persist. Al-Tabrisi also reports blindness of heart followed by torment."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q08", "question": "How does the reply work as dialogue and ellipsis?", "turns_on": "These notes address different features of the same dialogue: the implied question and the omitted reciprocal terms.", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q08/p1", "position": "The reply answers the person's question about blindness and implicitly asks what he did to merit it.", "reasons": "Yahya says God explains that the signs came in worldly life. Al-Alusi supplies the implicit question 'What did I do?' before the charge that signs came and were forgotten. Ibn ʿAshur says the question starts a new sentence and God's reply is separated because it continues the dialogue. Al-Tabatabaʾi says 'thus' answers the blindness question; Asad recounts the sinner's complaint that he is blind despite earlier sight."}, {"id": "20:126/q08/p2", "position": "The wording leaves reciprocal blindness and abandonment implicit.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAshur identifies three ellipses: the gathering leaves him forgotten, the reply implies earlier blindness to signs, and it implies present blindness."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q09", "question": "Was this verse reported to have been revealed about a named person?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q09/p1", "position": "A report says it was revealed concerning al-Murshi.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAtiyya reports the attribution without further detail in the note."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q10", "question": "What reported warnings concern forgetting memorized Qur'an?", "turns_on": "The reports differ in the warned consequence and include differing transmitters and assessments of the Anas and ʿUbada routes.", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q10/p1", "position": "A Qur'an learner who later forgets it meets God maimed; one version joins this to a warning about rulers over ten.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports the Prophetic warning that a ruler over ten comes shackled until freed by justice and a forgetful Qur'an learner meets God ajdham. Ahmad transmits the latter from Saʿd ibn ʿUbada and also through ʿUbada ibn al-Samit. Ibn Kathir notes Abu ʿAwana's ʿUbada transmission through Yazid and disagreement in its chain; he accepts it for exhortation if corroborated, as Abu ʿUbayd says."}, {"id": "20:126/q10/p2", "position": "Forgetting an entrusted Qur'anic verse or surah is described as the community's greatest sin.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir gives Anas's report that the Prophet saw his community's rewards, even removing dirt from a mosque, and saw no greater sin; a report attributed to Salman similarly names an entrusted surah. The fuller Anas version passes through Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, Abu Yaʿla, al-Bazzar, and others; al-Tirmidhi calls it gharīb, al-Bukhari finds it strange, al-Darimi questions al-Mutallib's hearing from Anas, and Ibn Kathir notes an alternate al-Zuhri route."}, {"id": "20:126/q10/p3", "position": "The Prophet commanded regular review because Qur'an slips from memory faster than camels escape.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites the Prophetic command and comparison."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q11", "question": "Does this verse condemn literal forgetting of memorized Qur'an as a major sin?", "turns_on": "Whether nasiya means culpable rejection or lost memorization, and whether the latter arose from negligence and disregard.", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q11/p1", "position": "The verse targets abandoning and disbelieving in the signs, not mere loss of memorized wording while one understands and practices it.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir says such loss is outside this particular threat, though another warning applies. Al-Alusi says the verse cannot establish that mere forgetting a Qur'anic verse is a major sin because nasiya means abandoning and not believing. Ibn ʿAtiyya and al-Tabrisi distinguish neglect from involuntary lapse, which is not punishable conduct."}, {"id": "20:126/q11/p2", "position": "Neglecting recitation, allowing Qur'an to be forgotten, and failing to care for it are grave parts of turning away from remembrance.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir reports this inclusion by some commentators and endorses it as a part, though not the whole, of the verse's intent. Abu Shama, as reported by al-Alusi, construes traditions condemning forgetfulness as failure to act on Qur'an."}, {"id": "20:126/q11/p3", "position": "Forgetting Qur'an or even a verse counts as a major sin, with literal forgetting qualified by laziness and disregard.", "reasons": "Al-Alusi reports al-Rafiʿi's major-sin ruling and says al-Nawawi's wording in al-Rawda seems to favor it. {"id": "20:126/q12", "question": "What practical warning does the verse give its hearers?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q12/p1", "position": "Reflect on God's signs, take heed, and stop heedless conduct lest the same fate follow.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri urges reflection, taking heed, and turning back from bad conduct. Ibn ʿAshur says the Qur'an cites the fate to warn its hearers against turning from remembrance. Bint al-Shati notes that ḍank appears only here in the Qur'an in this warning, whose subjects are raised blind. Al-Razi says a worldly reading of constricted life pairs hardship in life with afterlife blindness for turning from remembrance."}]}
{"id": "20:126/q13", "question": "How do decree and human effort relate to the warning?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q13/p1", "position": "Happiness and misery are decreed and foreknown, yet striving and effort are also within the decree.", "reasons": "Al-Qushayri says divine knowledge encompasses what will occur and still urges effort."}]}

{"id": "20:126/q16", "question": "What other passages illuminate being forgotten and later seeing punishment?", "turns_on": "The cited parallels illuminate different aspects of the fate: reciprocal abandonment and eventual sight of punishment.", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q16/p1", "position": "Other verses describe God forgetting those who forgot their meeting with the Day.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathir cites 7:51 for reciprocal forgetting. 17", "question": "What general rhetorical observations are recorded alongside this verse?", "turns_on": "These are distinct rhetorical observations, not competing readings of the verse.", "positions": [{"id": "20:126/q17/p1", "position": "Readerly misapprehension ranges from firm false belief to a fleeting impression, depending on how strong the resemblance is.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani distinguishes degrees of resemblance and their effects on a listener."}, {"id": "20:126/q17/p2", "position": "A phrase is empty padding only if it contributes nothing; an unexpected benefit makes it meaningful.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani distinguishes condemned padding from a phrase that initially seems expendable but benefits the listener."}, {"id": "20:126/q17/p3", "position": "Metaphor is a form of simile and representation, an analogy grasped by intellect and heart.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani says comparison is not apprehended by hearing alone."}, {"id": "20:126/q17/p4", "position": "Antithesis depends on opposed meanings rather than merely opposed word forms.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani locates antithesis in the ideas expressed."}, {"id": "20:126/q17/p5", "position": "Word order can disrupt comprehension when it fails to follow the order of thought.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjani uses a line of al-Farazdaq: the hearer must rearrange it, disrupting the image like ill-assembled geometric parts."}]}
{"id": "20:127/q01", "question": "What earlier punishment does ‘and thus’ point back to?", "turns_on": "The antecedent of ‘thus’ and the point at which the narrative turns to its audience.", "positions": [{"id": "20:127/q01/p1", "position": "It applies the preceding punishment of those who turned from God's signs to others who exceed the bounds and disbelieve.", "reasons": "Jishumi calls this an analogy to the warning about turning from the Qur'an. Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies the narrow life of 20:124 as the comparison; Ṭabāṭabāʾī points to those who forgot the signs after warning in 20:124 and 20:126. Al-Ālūsī says a general class of punishment is compared with the particular punishment just described. Al-Samīn says ‘thus’ means in the manner of that punishment. Al-Qurṭubī includes turning from reflection on created things. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that the preceding dialogue leaves implicit the person's being forgotten and earlier blindness to the signs as well as present blindness."}, {"id": "20:127/q01/p2", "position": "It carries the lesson of the Adam and Satan account into the address to the Prophet and his community.", "reasons": "Jishumi reports Abū Muslim: the account of Satan ends here and its lesson is applied to the Prophet's people."}]}
{"id": "20:127/q02", "question": "Is this clause continued divine rebuke or a concluding statement to listeners?", "turns_on": "Whether the conjunction carries on the divine address or introduces a parenthetical conclusion.", "positions": [{"id": "20:127/q02/p1", "position": "It is a concluding lesson addressed to listeners, introduced parenthetically by the conjunction.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr presents this as an alternative to continuing God's address to the resurrected man; on this reading the afterlife comparison concludes the story by referring back to the worldly hardship of 20:124. Ṭabāṭabāʾī also takes the wāw as opening a new statement, without specifying its addressee."}, {"id": "20:127/q02/p2", "position": "It continues God's rebuke addressed to the person resurrected blind.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the conjunction then links this clause to the previous sentence; the man's afterlife punishment is worse and longer than worldly punishment."}]}
{"id": "20:127/q03", "question": "What requital does God promise in ‘We requite’?", "turns_on": "Whether the statement is specified by the earlier punishment or described across both lives.", "positions": [{"id": "20:127/q03/p1", "position": "God gives comparable punishment to those who transgress and reject His signs.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī, al-Wāḥidī in al-Wajīz, al-Baghawī, Ibn ʿAṭiyya, al-Ṭabrisī, al-Nasafī, al-Samīn, al-Biqāʿī, al-Ālūsī, Ibn ʿĀshūr, and Ṭabāṭabāʾī apply the preceding warning to this class. Al-Bursawī and al-Ālūsī describe the response as corresponding to the offense; al-Biqāʿī includes arrogant defiance by denial or by acting like a denier. Al-Ṭabarī identifies the constricted grave-life as the requital. Al-Wāḥidī reports Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Kalbī, and the exegetes: the one who abandoned the signs is left in the Fire today."}, {"id": "20:127/q03/p2", "position": "The deniers are requited in this life and the next.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr cites 13:34 for punishment in both lives. Asad describes the eventual recompense as severe, enduring punishment in the life to come."}]}
{"id": "20:127/q04", "question": "What does ‘exceeded’ mean here?", "turns_on": "Whether isrāf is specified as shirk and unbelief, taken broadly as crossing a limit in conduct, or characterized by pursuit of desire.", "positions": [{"id": "20:127/q04/p1", "position": "It means associating partners with God, unbelief, or stubborn denial of His signs.", "reasons": "Muqātil, Yaḥyā ibn Sallām, Ibn ʿAbbās as reported by al-Wāḥidī, al-Wāḥidī's al-Wajīz, al-Thaʿlabī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, and Sufyān as reported by al-Durr specify shirk. Al-Rāzī reports this as one interpretation and takes the following denial of signs as explaining the excess. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies false belief, unbelief, and stubborn denial; Ṭabāṭabāʾī says rejecting signs transgresses the bounds of servitude. Al-Ṭabrisī joins shirk to disobedience."}, {"id": "20:127/q04/p2", "position": "It means going beyond limits through disobedience or sin, including misuse of one's capacities.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports disobedience as another interpretation. Al-Ṭabarī says disobeying God; al-Qurṭubī says transgressing through sin. Al-Bursawī defines isrāf as exceeding the limit in any human action, though it is most familiar in spending. Ṭabāṭabāʾī and Iṣlāḥī define it as exceeding a limit; Iṣlāḥī says people waste talents on forbidden things and neglect obligations. Asad refers to his discussion of the cognate musrif in sūra 10 and renders the offenders as wasting themselves; Study Quran refers readers to 10:12."}, {"id": "20:127/q04/p3", "position": "It means plunging into desires and turning away from the signs or God's commands.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī speaks of appetites; al-Biqāʿī of following desire and arrogantly rejecting commands; al-Ālūsī of plunging into desires and denying or turning away from signs."}]}
{"id": "20:127/q05", "question": "What are ‘the signs of his Lord’?", "turns_on": "Whether ‘signs’ is restricted to the Qur'an or includes other divine proofs and communications.", "positions": [{"id": "20:127/q05/p1", "position": "They are the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Muqātil identifies the signs as the Qur'an; al-Qurṭubī includes turning from the Qur'an in the offense."}, {"id": "20:127/q05/p2", "position": "They include God's proofs, scriptures, messengers, and miracles, including the Qur'an.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī names messengers and books; al-Ṭabrisī names proofs, scriptures, and messengers; al-Bursawī names the Qur'an and other miracles. Al-Qurṭubī also includes reflection on created things in what the sinner turns away from."}]}
{"id": "20:127/q06", "question": "What does failing to believe the signs involve?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "20:127/q06/p1", "position": "It is refusing to affirm the signs, denying or abandoning them, and potentially acting against them.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī says failing to affirm them as true; al-Bayḍāwī adds denial and acting contrary to them. Al-Bursawī says denial and turning away. Al-Ṭabarī specifies rejection of messengers and books.
